a-20g: An American strike aircraft present since the open beta, it was first modelled as the A-20G-30 and became the A-20G-25 when Update 1.47 "Big Guns" reworked it. Its forward guns match many US fighters for punch, good for strafing soft targets or winning head-on passes, and three 12.7 mm defensive guns guard the rear. It turns badly and bleeds energy quickly, so avoid dogfights: stay low and fast and let the dorsal turret do the work. As a strike aircraft it spawns lower than bombers and gets no bomb sight in Realistic battles.
a-26b: The A-26B-50 was a late-war Invader best known for its fourteen nose-mounted Browning machine guns and racks for HVAR rockets; 109 were built, and the USAF kept flying them into the late 1960s. Added in Update 1.67 "Assault", it uses that wall of guns to shred aircraft and lightly armoured ground or naval targets in a short burst. Compared with the A-26B-10 it gives up a little speed and climb for slightly better handling, but it remains a fast, heavy attacker with a similar bomb load plus the rocket option.
a-26b_10: Douglas designed the A-26 Invader to follow the A-20 Havoc, with an interchangeable nose that made it either a glazed bomber (A-26C) or a gun-nosed attacker (A-26B); it served from 1944 into the Vietnam era and was briefly renamed B-26 after 1946. The A-26B-10, added in Update 1.71 "New E.R.A.", carries six nose .50 cals, up to 4,000 lb of bombs and two remote twin-.50 turrets that track vertical manoeuvres well. Modifications can replace guns with one or two 37 mm cannons, giving a fast but unwieldy airframe a much heavier punch.
a-26c: The glazed-nose bomber version of the Invader, the A-26C-45 dates from the open beta and was handed out as a gift in the 2013 Memorial Day and Indian Summer events and the 2016 Mastermind Quiz. A top speed of around 569 km/h is exceptional for a piston bomber, letting it reach distant targets early, and 4,000 lb of bombs in several loadouts keep it flexible. Eight .50 cal guns handle soft targets or an unlucky fighter, and two remote twin-.50 turrets give accurate defensive fire that the Mosquito lacks.
a-26c-45-dt: A PlayStation-only premium sold as part of a special pack, the A-26C-45DT is an Invader bomber modified to carry HVAR rockets. At around 569 km/h it outruns the comparable Tu-2 by roughly 200 km/h, so it can strike deep targets before most rivals arrive, carrying up to 4,000 lb of bombs in a range of configurations. Eight forward .50 cals deal with soft targets, and two remotely controlled twin-.50 turrets give it accurate protection that unarmed fast bombers such as the Mosquito do without.
a-35b: Vultee's Model 72 began in 1940 as a dive-bomber ordered by the French Air Force; after France fell it evolved into the American A-35 Vengeance, and almost 70 A-35A/Bs later reached France under Lend-Lease. In the French tree since Update 1.73 "Vive la France", it is a capable ground attacker whose best loadout is four 500 lb bombs. Six .50 cal guns with 375 rounds each give about 30 seconds of fire for soft targets and light pillboxes, and steel plates shield the crew and oil cooler, but a lone rear 12.7 mm gun is its only defence.
a2d: The Douglas A2D-1 Skyshark was a US Navy turboprop attack aircraft meant to replace the Skyraider; constant trouble with its Allison XT40A engine and gearbox delayed the first flight to May 1950 and led to cancellation in 1954, after two prototypes and ten pre-production airframes. Since Update 1.89 "Imperial Navy" it has proven very versatile: quick and agile enough to contest early jets, armed with four 20 mm cannons, and able to carry a wide choice of bombs and rockets that threaten tanks in mixed battles, despite its bulky frame.
a5m4: Mitsubishi's Type 96 carrier fighter, designed by Jiro Horikoshi's team before they created the Zero, became the first monoplane anywhere to fly from carriers when adopted in 1936, outclassing Chinese P-26s before meeting the faster I-16. In the game since the open beta, the A5M4 is one of the nimblest monoplanes at the low ranks, able to out-turn and evade most opponents, and its airframe stands up reasonably well to normal ammunition. Firepower is its weakness: two 7.7 mm machine guns take a long time to bring anything down.
a5m4_hagiri: Matsuo Hagiri flew this A5M4, coded W-102, with the carrier Sōryū's fighter unit and became an ace over China and later in the Pacific war, claiming eight Chinese aircraft in it and in an early A6M during combat trials. Added in Update 1.31, it shares the standard A5M4's character: outstanding low-rank agility for dodging and out-turning enemies and a fairly durable airframe. The drawback is the same pair of 7.7 mm machine guns, which deal little damage per pass.
a6m2_mod11: The Model 11 was the pre-production Zero sent to China for combat trials, lacking a tail hook, folding wingtips and drop-tank fittings; on debut, 13 of them downed 27 I-15s and I-16s within minutes without loss, and mass production as the Model 21 followed. Added in Update 1.39, it turns superbly and its two 20 mm cannons hit hard, though shells are few and slow. With no armour or self-sealing tanks it must dodge diving attacks rather than absorb them and cannot chase faster foes, yet it is less outpaced by its usual opponents than the later A6M5s.
a6m2_n_zero: The A6M2-N, or Type 2 seaplane fighter, was a stopgap while the N1K1 lagged behind: a Model 11 Zero with a modified tail and three floats, the central one holding extra fuel. It came too late for the island offensives it was meant for, but served on patrol and defence because it needed no airfield. In the game since the open beta, it shares the A6M2 Model 11's guns and engine but flies worse under the weight of the pontoons, which can be shot away, torn off by overspeed or lost on the ground, restoring much of the normal Zero's handling.
a6m2_zero: The Model 21 was the Zero most Allied pilots met early in the war, fighting at Pearl Harbor, Midway and the Aleutians before the Hellcat and Corsair overtook it. In the game since the open beta, it adds carrier equipment (hook, folding wingtips and drop-tank mounts) to the Model 11 yet flies the same way: a superb turner whose 20 mm cannons are powerful but slow and short of shells. Without armour or self-sealing tanks it must dodge diving attacks and cannot catch faster fighters, though it is outpaced less often than the later A6M5s.
a6m2_zero_china: Chinese Nationalist and Communist forces both captured Model 21 Zeros; this one probably represents V-172 and V-174, which force-landed on the Leizhou Peninsula in 1941 and became the first Zeros in Allied hands, studied just before the Pacific War. Added in Update 1.93 "Shark Attack", it is identical to the Japanese A6M2, pairing excellent agility with powerful cannons that carry little ammunition. The airframe is fragile and hits to the fuel tanks start fires easily, so keep enough energy to climb away rather than turning indefinitely.
a6m2_zero_usa: This is the "Akutan Zero", an almost intact A6M2 found crashed in Alaska in July 1942, then repaired and flight-tested in the United States to reveal weaknesses Allied pilots could exploit; it was wrecked in February 1945 when an SB2C Helldiver ran into it during training. In the game since the open beta, it performs exactly like the Japanese A6M2 and differs mainly in its US Navy-style paint. Its agility makes it easy to line up shots, but with only 60 rounds per 20 mm cannon it demands far more trigger discipline than the ammunition-rich American fighters around it.
a6m3_mod22_zero: The Model 22 put the full-span folding wings of the Model 21 back on the A6M3, kept the Sakae 21 engine and 100-round cannon drums of the Model 32, and added outer-wing tanks to recover range; 560 were built between December 1942 and mid-1943 for the Solomons and New Guinea campaigns. In the game since the open beta, it handles like the Models 11 and 21 again, with a little more power at altitude and more 20 mm ammunition, but meets somewhat stronger opposition. Like every Zero, it rules low-altitude turning fights yet has no armour or self-sealing tanks and cannot catch faster enemies.
a6m3_mod22ko_zero: The Model 22Kō is an A6M3 Model 22 whose only change is a switch from the Type 99 Model 1 to the Model 2 20 mm cannon, which has a longer barrel, chamber and cartridge. Introduced in Update 1.37, it flies like the other full-wing Zeros, but the new gun raises muzzle velocity from 600 to 750 m/s, so shells drop less and reach the target sooner while hitting just as hard. The result is noticeably easier gunnery than on earlier models.
a6m3_zero: The Model 32 was the first big Zero upgrade, gaining the two-speed supercharged Sakae 21 engine and clipped wings without folding tips; roll rate and dive speed improved, but range fell by almost 1,000 km and turning suffered, shortcomings exposed over the Solomons that led to the Model 22. In the game since the open beta, it carries 100 rounds per 20 mm cannon and gains a little top speed and roll rate. The clipped wings reward pilots who prefer boom-and-zoom, while traditional Zero turn-fighters will notice its wider turns.
a6m5_zero: The Model 52 was the last mass-produced Zero, with shorter rounded wingtips, individual exhaust stacks that added thrust, more armour and, in later batches, self-sealing tanks, plus the improved Type 99 Model 2 cannon. In the game since the open beta, it outperforms earlier Zeros but meets opponents that have improved even more. It still out-turns nearly anything, yet most enemies are faster, so staying behind them is harder work. Like the other A6M5s, it can swap the centreline drop tank for a 250 kg bomb as a "bakusen" fighter-bomber.
a6m5hei: The Model 52 Hei was the final A6M5 sub-variant: it added a 13.2 mm Type 3 gun in each wing and four rocket racks, dropped the last 7.7 mm, and thickened the protection for the wings and pilot, and the extra weight kept it mostly to B-29 interception and special-attack missions. Added in Update "Ixwa Strike", it gives up the Zero's trademark agility for firepower, ordnance and toughness. Classic turn-fighting rarely works, so it is best flown with boom-and-zoom passes, against bombers or in ground attack.
a6m5ko: The Model 52 Kō was the first sub-variant of the A6M5, switching to belt-fed Type 99 cannons that raise total ammunition from 200 to 250 rounds. In the game since the open beta, it shares the A6M5's traits: superb in a turning fight but outpaced by most opponents, which makes staying on an enemy's tail harder. The extra cannon rounds allow a few more attacks, and the "bakusen" option adds a 250 kg bomb. It left the store after the 2023 Summer sale and briefly returned for Golden Eagles during a 2024 National Foundation Day event.
a6m5otsu: The Model 52 Otsu kept the Kō's belt-fed cannons with 125 rounds each, swapped one 7.7 mm for a 13.2 mm Type 3 machine gun, and added a 45 mm armoured windscreen and a larger spinner. Introduced in Update 1.37, it flies like the other A6M5s, turning brilliantly but struggling to keep up with faster rivals. The heavy machine gun adds to the combined damage and leaves a useful weapon once the cannons run dry, and a 250 kg bomb can be fitted for the "bakusen" role.
a6m6c: The A6M6 Model 53 was a prototype based on the Model 52 Hei, testing the Sakae 31a engine with water-methanol boost; the extra power was slight and the engine proved unreliable, though the type did gain self-sealing tanks. It arrived in Update "Red Skies" as a reward from Battle Pass Season IV, "Fearless Voltigeur". Heavier and less agile than any other Zero, it compensates with better protection and firepower, forgiving mistakes and suiting boom-and-zoom or fast fights with sudden snap turns, while ample machine-gun ammunition and a bomb load make ground attack viable.
a7he1: Japan's Navy bought surplus German He 112 B-0 fighters as the A7He1 to reinforce its air arm in China; faster and better armed than the A5M but less agile and slower to climb, they did not fit naval doctrine and were kept only for study. Added in Update 1.37, it offers an unusual style for the Japanese tree, built on a 690 km/h top speed and a pair of 20 mm cannons backed by two quick-firing 7.92 mm guns. Its climb is mediocre, and it is neither nimble nor quick to respond.
a7m1: The A7M1 (NK9H) was a pre-production Reppū, the Zero's intended successor, fitted with Nakajima's Homare engine because Mitsubishi's own Ha-43 was not ready; it flew in May 1944 and handled well, but was underpowered and the Navy cancelled it. Added in Update 1.53 "Firestorm", it sits before the A7M2 in the tree and is a genuine all-rounder. Strong energy retention, a very tight turn and respectable speed let it work as either a turn fighter or an energy fighter, so it fits almost any style.
a7m2: Mitsubishi designed the A7M2 Reppū to outdo the Zero in firepower, speed, climb and dive; engine choices and wing-loading problems dragged development out, and only nine were finished before the war ended, none reaching service. Added in Update 1.55 "Royal Armour", it keeps much of the Zero's agility while being faster and far better armed, so it suits novices and veterans alike and can run down more targets than an A6M. Its rockets, which have a distance fuse, work against both aircraft and ground targets but weigh it down, so carry them only when needed.
a_109_eoa2: Agusta, known for motorcycles as well as helicopters such as the AB-205 and A129, created the A109 mainly to break into export markets; conceived for civil use, it was soon adapted for military work, with a military prototype shown in 1973 and later TOW integration. Added in Update "Hot Tracks", it flies better than most helicopters it meets and its roomy airframe absorbs some hits, carrying up to four missiles plus gun or rocket pods. Unlocking the TOWs is the hard part, as the stock rockets are few and imprecise, and with no countermeasures it is easy prey for SAMs.
a_10a_early: Fairchild Republic built the A-10A Thunderbolt II around the enormous 30 mm GAU-8 Avenger, protecting the pilot in a titanium tub and giving it redundant controls and rugged TF34 turbofans; it first fought in the 1991 Gulf War. A premium since Update "Wind of Change", it is heavy, underpowered and slow, so fighters and anti-aircraft remain dangerous despite its armour, though a large countermeasure supply helps against missiles. Mavericks, guided and unguided bombs and rockets fill its pylons, the cannon has deep ammunition and strong penetration, and two AIM-9Ls offer some self-defence.
a_10a_late: The A-10 grew from Vietnam-era lessons that the A-1 was obsolete and the F-4 too expensive for close support; built around a new rotary 30 mm cannon, it entered production in 1973, took the Thunderbolt II name in 1978 and first saw combat in 1991, later serving over Iraq and Afghanistan. Added in Update "Wind of Change" alongside the premium A-10A, the Late version lacks guided bombs but brings AGM-65D Mavericks, Hydra rockets, varied bombs and four all-aspect AIM-9Ls. Its sluggish flight performance means it must be flown with care.
a_10c: From 2005 the A-10 fleet received the Precision Engagement Modification, which brought a new fire-control system and displays, the LITENING II targeting pod, Paveway II and JDAM bombs and newer Mavericks; around 350 airframes had been converted by 2011. The A-10C, which arrived in Update "Dance of the Dragons", adds a helmet-mounted cueing system, laser-guided Paveways, all-weather JDAMs that cannot engage moving targets, high-explosive AGM-65G/L missiles and AIM-9Ms for air threats. Its low top speed and general sluggishness remain the biggest drawback.
a_129_a: Agusta developed the A-129 International as an export version of the Mangusta with new engines, weapons and avionics; no country bought it, but the lessons went into the Italian Army's A129CBT upgrade. Added in Update 1.93 "Shark Attack", it carries Hellfire ATGMs and Hydra rockets alongside a .50 cal turret for aircraft and soft targets. Stronger engines make it agile, quick to reach top speed and capable at height, but it has no flares, chaff or air-to-air missiles, so it does best when the sky is free of enemy aircraft and anti-air.
a_129_cbt: When the export A129 International found no buyers, Italy, Spain, Britain and the Netherlands agreed in 1986 to develop an improved Joint European Helicopter; the partners left for the Apache and Tiger in 1990, but Italy used the work to field the A129CBT with modern avionics, later deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan. Added in Update "Hot Tracks", it accelerates briskly and handles well at low speed, so it can strike and slip away quickly. AGM-114B Hellfires are its main punch, Mistral missiles chase air targets far better than ATAS, and a three-barrel 20 mm cannon handles light targets.
a_129_d: Italy's AH-129D (Delta) programme upgraded 32 A129CBTs from 2014 with new avionics and the fire-and-forget SPIKE ER missile, aimed through a Rafael TOP LITE sight that removed the ability to fire TOWs; the type served in Afghanistan until the 2021 withdrawal. Added in Update "Kings of Battle", it differs from the CBT mainly in weapons: SPIKEs lock onto any kind of target and can be launched at several in quick succession, potentially eight in one sortie, though the missiles are slow. Otherwise it keeps the CBT's agility, acceleration and broad mix of air-to-ground and air-to-air armament.
a_20g_30_ussr: The Soviet Union received 3,414 A-20 Havocs under Lend-Lease, more than the USAAF itself operated, and its engineers added extra racks that roughly doubled the bomb load at some cost to performance; crews liked the type for its speed, agility and easy upkeep. Added in Update "Fire and Ice", the Soviet A-20G-30 is a nimbler option than the Lend-Lease B-25J, carrying far bigger and heavier bombs than American Havocs for base bombing and close support. It is less survivable, though, and otherwise matches the American version, so faster, more modern opponents punish it, especially when it is fully loaded.
a_29_hudson: Lockheed turned its Model 14 Super Electra airliner into the Hudson reconnaissance bomber, first for Britain; the A-29 variant used Wright R-1820 engines, and China received 26, though accidents claimed many and few saw combat. Added in Update 1.91 "Night Vision", it is a serviceable light bomber let down by its guns: one 12.7 mm and one 7.62 mm turret for defence, and two forward 7.62 mm guns good only for soft targets such as AA or artillery positions. Its best escape is a dive, as the airframe holds together up to about 564 km/h.
a_4b: Ed Heinemann at Douglas designed the A-4 Skyhawk as a small, light, cheap and easily maintained Navy attacker; over 540 A-4Bs were built, gaining improved navigation and AGM-12 Bullpup missiles, and the type flew as the Navy's main light bomber over Vietnam. Added in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury", it is a nimble multirole jet whose options stretch to 5,000 lb of bombs, as many as 133 unguided rockets, or a gun-heavy fit of five 20 mm cannons sharing 2,350 rounds. Heavy loads blunt its agility, but it works well at low and medium altitude, particularly when attacking ground targets.
a_4e_early: The A-4E (A4D-5) brought the stronger and much more fuel-efficient J52-P-6A engine and new AJB-3A and Mk 9 bombing systems, with later aircraft adding the avionics hump and J52-P-8. The Early version, a squadron vehicle from Update "New Power", is as useful in a dogfight as in ground attack. Its ordnance ranges from unguided bombs and rockets to AGM-62A Walleye guided bombs, with CCRP toss-bombing but no CCIP. In the air it is nimble enough to take on most contemporaries, and two AIM-9Bs plus flares help when facing missiles such as the AIM-9G and R-60.
a_4e_early_iaf: The A-4E (A4D-5) introduced the more efficient and powerful J52-P-6A, extra pylons and new navigation and bombing computers; Early aircraft lacked the later avionics hump and J52-P-8 engine. Israel received more than 25 of them to make good heavy Skyhawk losses in the Yom Kippur War. Added in Update "Winged Lions", it is effectively a slightly less capable take on the premium Israeli A-4E, with about 8% less thrust. Two chin-mounted 30 mm DEFA cannons and two AIM-9Bs give it teeth, and 60 countermeasures are valuable when Sea Vixens are around and in matches full of AIM-9Gs and R-60s.
a_4e_late_iaf: The A-4E was a big step for the Skyhawk, with better avionics, a stronger engine and six pylons; Israel, its largest export user, received 46 from the US to replace aircraft lost in the Yom Kippur War. Sold as a premium pack from Update "Ground Breaking", it is fast and well armed enough to fight, yet carries enough bombs, rockets and AGM-62A guided bombs to wipe out two bases in Air RB. Its AIM-9Bs punish slow targets stuck in dogfights, many of which lack flares, and 60 countermeasures offset how quickly it loses energy. It left the store after the 2023 May sale.
a_4h: Turned down in 1963, Israel's request for Skyhawks was approved three years later, producing the A-4H: an A-4E adapted for land bases, with the J52-P-8A engine and two 30 mm DEFA cannons instead of 20 mm guns; about 90 served until the F-16 replaced them. Added in Update "Winged Lions", it is strong in both air combat and ground attack thanks to a light airframe, a good thrust-to-weight ratio and cannons that wreck aircraft, soft targets and even some medium tanks. It has no air-to-air missiles and no guided air-to-ground weapons, though its range of unguided loadouts is wide.
a_4n: The A-4N Ayit was Israel Aircraft Industries' 1980s modernisation of the IAF's Skyhawks to roughly US Marine A-4M standard, adding an Elbit HUD and computers, an Elta radar and compatibility with later Sidewinders and Mavericks; it served into the early 2000s. Added in Update "Winged Lions", it is the most capable Skyhawk in the game and a force in mixed battles, with a stronger engine, dangerous infrared missiles and early AGM-65A Mavericks that outrange most air defences it meets. In pure air battles it struggles against supersonic jets and opponents with countermeasures, so pick off distracted or isolated fighters instead.
a_4ptm_malaysia: In 1979 Malaysia ordered 88 surplus US Navy A-4Cs and A-4Ls, but money limited the upgrade to 43 single-seaters and six two-seaters, designated A-4PTM, with a Saab RGS-2A gunsight, more weapon options, a drag chute and a refuelling probe. Unreliable in service, they gave way to BAE Hawks and were gone by 1999. Added to the Japanese tree in Update 2.59 "Sky Odyssey", it resembles the Israeli Ayit, with strong air-to-air missiles, but can only attack ground targets with bombs, taking it into SAM range. It turns respectably but lacks speed and acceleration and bleeds energy in turns.
a_5c: The A-5C was the export Q-5 Fantan, born from a Pakistani request in the early 1980s, when China was starting to sell arms rather than donate them; it combined the Q-5's strong low-level performance and low price with Western electronics and armament, and was sold to several countries. Added in Update "Direct Hit", it flies like the Q-5A and keeps its ballistic computer for rockets and bombs, but gains dedicated wing pylons for Magic 1 or AIM-9P missiles. Climbing very well for a strike jet and with slightly better agility than its contemporaries, this MiG-19 derivative can surprise opponents in air combat.
a_6e_tram: Grumman's A-6 Intruder won a 1958 competition for an all-weather Navy and Marine attack aircraft and served from 1963 to 1997; the A-6E of 1972 improved its navigation, attack and radar systems, and the 1979 TRAM package added sensors for better targeting. A premium since Update "Apex Predators", it has no built-in gun and relies entirely on five customisable hardpoints, and TRAM lets it drop guided bombs without a targeting pod. Being subsonic, it is slow to reach the fight, closer to the A-10 and Su-25 in style, but few aircraft can tailor a loadout so precisely to the task.
a_7d: LTV based the A-7 Corsair II on the F-8 Crusader, making it smaller and subsonic to save cost as the Navy's A-4 replacement; the USAF's A-7D of 1968 added a TF41 engine, better avionics and an M61 rotary cannon, with over 450 built and service into the early 1990s. Added in Update "Hot Tracks", it carries a single M61 and eight pylons for a wide range of bombs, rockets and missiles, including precision-guided weapons. It can defend itself when it must, but as a subsonic jet among many supersonic interceptors it is far better suited to ground attack than air battles.
a_7e: Impressed by the Air Force's A-7D, the US Navy had Vought build the A-7E with the TF41 engine, the M61A1 cannon, better avionics and more hardpoints; first flown in March 1969, 529 were built and it fought over Vietnam, Libya and in Desert Storm before the F/A-18 replaced it. Added in Update "Ground Breaking", it lacks the A-7D's GBU-8 and AGM-65 but brings the LANA FLIR pod and TV-guided AGM-62A Walleye I ER bombs, letting it destroy armour quickly and accurately even on night maps. Success depends on reading the enemy's air defences and knowing the ground battle well enough to find targets fast.
a_7e_greece: Greece bought 60 A-7Hs in 1975–80 to replace its F-84Fs and liked them enough to add 62 ex-US Navy A-7Es in 1993; they never saw combat, and Greece was the last nation to retire the type, in 2014. Placed in the Israeli tree in Update 2.59 "Sky Odyssey", it is, like the American and Japanese-tree A-7Es, far more effective striking ground targets than fighting. Weak thrust and a modest top speed matter little in that role, while a broad choice of guided air-to-surface weapons and an infrared targeting pod let it attack from beyond the reach of enemy air defences.
a_7e_thailand: The Royal Thai Navy acquired retired US Navy A-7Es, plus TA-7E trainers, in the mid-1990s to modernise its strike capability, basing them with the 104th Squadron at U-Tapao. Maintenance demands, training and limited resources kept them from settling in, and they went into storage in 2007, the last A-7Es in service outside the United States. Added in Update "Storm Warning", it matches the American A-7E with the LANA FLIR pod and TV-guided Walleye bombs for precise attacks on armour, but mediocre flight performance makes it easy prey for SAMs and fighters; two AIM-9Gs offer some self-defence.
a_7h_greece: The A-7H was the Hellenic Air Force's version of the A-7E without aerial refuelling; Greece bought 60 between 1975 and 1980 to replace F-84Fs, valued them for their simplicity and handling, and retired them in 2007 without combat use. Introduced to the Israeli tree in Update 2.59 "Sky Odyssey", it is the weakest Corsair in the game because it has no guided air-to-surface weapons. That leaves it short of power and speed as a fighter and unable to strike from outside air-defence range as an attacker.
a_7k: A two-seat A-7D variant with a stretched nose, the A-7K was made for Air National Guard units, mainly as a trainer; 30 were made, and the in-game version reflects 1980s aircraft fitted with a thermal sight. Players earned it through the "Repair Factory" event during Update "Sky Guardians". That thermal sight gives it a real edge on the A-7D in the tree for spotting targets at range, though its guided weapons, the Maverick B and GBU-8 Hobo, still cannot be used at night. AIM-9L missiles make it better armed for air threats than the D or E, although they serve only for self-defence.
ab_205a_1: Agusta obtained a licence in 1966 to build and export the UH-1, first as the AB-204 and then the stretched AB-205, whose cabin seats up to 14; the more powerful, armed AB-205A-1 entered Italian military service. Added in Update "Hot Tracks" as the first Italian helicopter, it is quicker and more agile than a standard UH-1 thanks to its stronger engine. Armament is thin, just 14 FFAR Mighty Mouse rockets and two 7.62 mm M134 miniguns, so success depends on accurate rocket fire, with the miniguns best kept for aircraft.
ah_1f: The AH-1F was the most advanced single-engine Cobra, the end point of a long upgrade programme after the AH-1G's Vietnam service, with a stronger engine and better navigation and electronic warfare gear; about 150 were built new and some 300 converted, and they fought in the 1991 Gulf War. Added in Update 1.81 "The Valkyries", it gains a HUD, an IRCM jammer and exhaust suppressor, an armoured tandem cockpit, a chin turret and stub wings for TOW missiles or Hydra rockets. One of the first Cobras with thermal imaging, it finds targets quickly in cluttered areas, but it carries no flares.
ah_1f_iaf: The Tzefa D/E was the IAF's final Cobra, essentially an AH-1F; fourteen US Army surplus aircraft arrived in 1996 to replace MD500 Defenders, flew mostly in support of ground forces and against point targets, and gave way to the AH-64A in 2013. Added in Update "Danger Zone", it pairs good ATGMs with excellent agility, out-turning most helicopters despite an unremarkable top speed. The 20 mm rotary cannon fires very fast but penetrates little, so main battle tanks are hard to hurt even from above while SPAA and light vehicles shred quickly. Thermal imaging and countermeasures help, ideally a mixed load of chaff and flares.
ah_1g: Bell built the AH-1G HueyCobra as a private venture, the Model 209, reusing UH-1 components when the Army urgently needed an interim gunship for Vietnam while the AAFSS programme stalled; after a first flight in September 1965 it won a production contract in April 1966. In the game since Update 1.81 "The Valkyries", it opens the US helicopter tree and is far more agile than the UH-1. It relies on unguided FFAR rockets with no ballistic computer and has no ATGMs, so every attack means flying close to the enemy, where SPAA is a constant threat that calls for careful approaches.
ah_1g_iaf: After the 1973 Yom Kippur War exposed a lack of rapid-response anti-armour forces, Israel received its first AH-1s, named Tzefa, in 1977, using them in Lebanon against armour and fortified positions and, in 1982, against Syrian forces. Added in Update "Danger Zone", the Tzefa A is identical to the American AH-1G: quick and fairly agile, but without ATGMs or a ballistic computer for its rockets, and its 7.62 mm miniguns and 20 mm cannon do little even to light armour. SPAA is deadly up close, so approach behind terrain and buildings, or in Arcade leave AA to ATGM-armed helicopters.
ah_1q_iaf: The Tzefa B was Israel's anti-tank version of the AH-1G, carrying eight BGM-71C TOW missiles to fill a gap in rapid anti-armour response; limited service began in 1975, with more delivered in 1979. Added in Update "Danger Zone" with the first Israeli helicopters, it has the speed and agility of other Cobras plus the TOWs the Tzefa A lacks, so it can fight both up close and at range. At distance, use its quick handling to change position often and duck behind cover before enemy SPAA finds it.
ah_1s: This Japanese AH-1S wears artwork of the Kisarazu Sisters, characters first drawn by a member of the JGSDF's 4th Anti-Tank Helicopter Unit and illustrated by Takashi Fujisawa for the unit's 20th anniversary; it was also the game's first vehicle with a female crew. A premium pack from Update 1.89 "Imperial Navy", it was withdrawn from sale following the 8th Anniversary Sale and came back for Golden Eagles in Update "Hot Tracks". It has thermal sights and eight TOW-2s, but their 3.75 km reach is shorter than most air defences, so it works best supporting the team, firing from cover and relocating.
ah_1s_early: The AH-1E, or AH-1S ECAS, was the 1978 Step 2 Cobra with a three-barrel 20 mm M197 nose cannon; 98 were built, and two went to Japan for trials that led to licence production of the Step 3 AH-1S. Added in Update "Starfighters", it lacks the later AH-1S's TOW-2s and thermal imaging. Its TOWs hit hard but reach only 3.75 km, less than the air defences it meets, so it acts as a missile carrier rather than a long-range sniper: hide behind terrain and pop up to fire while the enemy holds the sky, and climb for a wider view only once teammates have cleared it.
ah_1s_late: Fuji Heavy Industries built 89 AH-1S Cobras under licence between 1984 and 2000, matching the US Army's Step 3 AH-1F and powered by the T53-K-703; the choice followed trials of two AH-1Es in 1977–78, and the type still serves with the JGSDF. Added in Update "Starfighters", it matches the AH-1S Kisarazu with eight TOW-2s and a thermal sight. The missiles' 3.75 km reach falls short of enemy air defences, so it works best as a supporting missile carrier, leaving SPAA, aircraft and helicopters to teammates.
ah_1w: The AH-1W Super Cobra, or "Whiskey Cobra", was a 1980s weapons and electronics upgrade of the twin-engine AH-1J Sea Cobra built for the US Marines, and it served alongside its AH-1Z Viper successor until 2020. Added in Update "Alpha Strike", it bridges the AH-1F and AH-1Z: wire-guided TOWs, a cannon and rockets suit fast attacks, while AGM-114B Hellfires, AIM-9Ls and thermal optics with automatic tracking support a more deliberate approach. It is also unusual in carrying large Zuni rockets, otherwise a fixed-wing weapon, for heavy high-explosive strikes.
ah_1w_china: Taiwan bought American AH-1Ws in 1992 to build new attack helicopter brigades; upgraded in the 2010s, they serve alongside the AH-64E Apache Guardian. Added in Update "Alpha Strike", the Taiwanese version brings plenty of Hellfires, AIM-9Ls and an autocannon for soft targets. It is not as fast or as strong against aircraft as its mainland counterparts in the Chinese tree, but it is quick and agile and more flexible than the Z-9 series. A missile approach warner fires countermeasures automatically, and an IRCM jammer disrupts infrared seekers.
ah_1z: The AH-1Z Viper developed the Super Cobra with four-blade composite rotors, main and tail, modern engines and better electronics; full-rate production was approved in late 2010, the Marines ordered 189 (131 of them converted AH-1Ws), and Bell delivered the last in November 2022. Added in Update 1.81 "The Valkyries", it is the most advanced Cobra in the game and quite unlike the rest: twin engines and the four-blade rotor make it faster and more responsive. Its wing stations take Hellfires, AIM-9Ms and laser-guided APKWS II Hydra rockets.
ah_2_rooivalk: With a UN embargo blocking imports during the Border War, South Africa had Denel develop its own attack helicopter from the Puma in 1984; the Rooivalk flew in 1990 but entered service only in 2011 after losing a 2007 Turkish contest to the A129, and eleven fly with 16 Squadron, including on UN duty in the DR Congo. Added to the British tree in Update "Drone Age" and dropped from the store after the 11th Anniversary sale, it rivals the Apaches, with laser and missile warning, thermal and night vision, tandem-warhead Mokopa ATGMs, all-aspect Mistral AAMs and a quick-firing 20 mm nose gun.
ah_56a: Lockheed's AH-56A Cheyenne won the Army's AAFSS contest in 1965 as a compound helicopter with a low wing and pusher propeller that reached nearly 400 km/h; complexity and sometimes fatal test crashes ended production plans in 1969 and the whole programme in 1972, the role later going to the Apache. Added in Update 2.51 "Spearhead", it rewards bold play: unrivalled speed and nimble handling put it in ambush positions fast, and a thermal imager, CCIP and a 30 mm cannon let it strike hard before ducking behind terrain. With no RWR, IRCM or countermeasures, being spotted is often fatal.
ah_60_iaf: The IAF has flown about 50 UH-60 Black Hawks on utility duties since trials in the 1980s, and rising demand for firepower led it to seek armed versions; the in-game model is the Elbit-upgraded AH-60L Arpía IV built for Colombia and shown in 2008 as the "Battle Hawk" demonstrator. Added in Update "Alpha Strike", the AH-60 "Yanshuf" brings the Black Hawk airframe to the Israeli tree. Its draw is a mixed load of up to 16 Spike fire-and-forget ATGMs and AGM-114K Hellfire IIs, backed by a GIAT M621 cannon that out-fires its rivals' guns, making it a real alternative to the Apaches and a big step up from the MD-500.
ah_64a: The AH-64A came out of the 1972 Advanced Attack Helicopter programme to replace the Cobra; the YAH-64 won in 1976, and its planned 16 TOWs became 16 of the longer-ranged, deadlier Hellfires developed alongside it. Over 900 were built, and many still serve in Greece, Israel, Saudi Arabia and elsewhere. Added in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury", it has one of the most flexible loadouts in the game, mixing Hydra and APKWS II rockets, Hellfires, AIM-9Ls and Stingers with a wide-arc M230 30 mm cannon firing HE-DP. A third-generation thermal imager and strong optics let it find and hit targets at any range while flying low to stay hidden.
ah_64a_greece_usa: Greece ordered 12 AH-64As in December 1991 and eight AH-64A+ in 1992; all 20 had arrived by 1995 and still serve with Hellenic Army Aviation alongside AH-64Ds bought in 2003. A premium in the US tree since Update "Fire and Ice", it carries the same weapons as the tree AH-64A, including Hellfires, Stingers and laser-guided APKWS II rockets whose 11 km reach makes them especially good against anti-aircraft vehicles. Premium bonuses speed up progress through the American helicopter line.
ah_64a_iaf: Israel invested in the Apache programme from 1983 and became the first country after the US to fly the AH-64A, known locally as Peten; up to 42 served, seeing action against Hezbollah in Lebanon. Added in Update "Danger Zone", it is a capable all-rounder in ground battles and helicopter PvE, with good handling, excellent optics and AGM-114B Hellfires that outrange most ATGMs and can attack from above, though they are less flexible than the Vikhr. It swaps the US version's AIM-9Ls for AIM-92 Stingers, which pull only 10 g but resist flares, and carries 1,200 rounds for its 30 mm cannon; just 60 countermeasures is its main weakness.
ah_64a_peten: Seeking to replace its MD-500s and AH-1s, Israel became the first export operator of the Apache, receiving its first AH-64As on 11 September 1990 and fielding 42 by 2000 under the name Peten. Added in Update "Wind of Change", this is an early Israeli configuration without many of the tree version's upgrades. It still carries laser-guided Hellfires, Hydra rockets and four ATAS missiles, handles well given its size and weight, and pairs a wide-arc 30 mm chin cannon firing dual-purpose shells with strong optics, a sharp thermal imager plus an IRST for engagements at any range.
ah_64a_peten_iaf: Israel's first Apaches arrived on 11 September 1990 and were assembled in only 11 hours for their welcome ceremony; the fleet grew to 42, flew many operations from Lebanon to the al-Aqsa Intifada, and was upgraded in 2013 to the AH-64Ai, close to D standard. Added in Update "Wind of Change", it handles well and carries 16 Hellfires, enough to keep fighting with enemy SPAA about. Its ATAS missiles lack agility but reach far and home accurately, so afterburning jets struggle to decoy them, and an IRCM jammer used together with flares and hard manoeuvring helps defeat IR missiles, even IRCCM types such as the R-73.
ah_64d: The AH-64D Apache Longbow grew from a US Army upgrade funded in 1991 and built around Northrop Grumman's AN/APG-78 radar above the rotor, which allowed bad-weather and over-water operation and simplified targeting; production began in 1995 with T700-GE-701C engines and new avionics, every Army AH-64A was converted, and over 1,000 were built. Added in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury", it handles like the AH-64A but gains AGM-114K Hellfire IIs and a missile warning system that releases countermeasures automatically. Its defining feature is the radar, which detects and tracks aircraft as well as ground vehicles.
ah_64d_i_saraph: The US blocked several Israeli orders for new AH-64Ds, named Saraph, amid investigations into misuse of American equipment against civilians, so most IAF AH-64As were brought up to D standard instead, gaining Hellfire IIs and better fire control; some have intercepted drones and other slow targets. Added in Update "Danger Zone", it keeps the Peten's good handling, strong ATGMs and fine optics, but adds the mast-mounted AN/APG-78 radar. The radar cannot lock targets, yet it reliably reveals nearby aircraft and helicopters flying above the terrain, and Hellfire IIs bring better guidance and a heavier charge.
ah_64d_japan: Fuji Heavy Industries licence-built the AH-64DJP as a cheaper alternative to a domestic design; plans for 62 shrank to just 12 as buying two a year drove up costs, and Japan decided in 2022 to replace its Apaches, AH-1Ss and OH-1s with drones. Added in Update "Starfighters", it mirrors the American AH-64D minus AMASE and APKWS. AGM-114K Hellfire IIs remain its main weapon: find targets with radar and thermals, then launch every five seconds or so to cover the long flight time or hit several targets. Four ATAS missiles handle air threats, and the 30 mm cannon's computer tracks and leads air and ground targets.
ah_64d_lightweight_japan: The AH-64D Longbow's mast-mounted AN/APG-78 radar, uprated engines and new avionics attracted Japan, where Fuji Heavy Industries signed in 2001 to licence-build 50 as the AH-64DJP; costs cut the run to thirteen, flown by the JGSDF, with targeting upgrades announced in 2017. Added as a premium in Update 2.55 "Ninth Wave", the AH-64DJP (AT) is the tree version without its radar. Everything else matches: a reasonably quick, well-armed Apache with long-range AGM-114K Hellfire IIs, AIM-92 Stingers and a helmet-mounted display.
ah_64d_netherlands: The Netherlands picked the AH-64D in 1995 over the Super Cobra, Mangusta and Tiger, ordering 30 without the Longbow radar but wired for it, and fitted them with Terma's AMASE self-protection pods on the wingtips; conversion of the fleet to AH-64E standard began in 2021. Added to the French tree in Update 2.43 "Storm Warning", it keeps the usual AH-64D weapons and systems, including missile warning and a helmet display that steers missiles wherever the pilot looks. The missing radar is the main difference; slow Hellfires and an imprecise 30 mm cannon are the familiar Apache drawbacks.
ah_64e: The AH-64E Apache Guardian began in 2004 as the AH-64D Block III and became its own model in 2012, adding the T700-GE-701D engine, an improved transmission, better networking including JTIDS, and composite rotor blades; at least 590 had been built or converted by January 2025. Added in Update "Tusk Force", it brings extra IRCM and new missiles: up to sixteen AGM-179s with 16 km range and IR or SAL guidance let it engage from safe distances. The IRCM pods sit permanently on the outer pylons, however, so those stations take only ATAS anti-air missiles, halving the anti-tank load.
ah_64e_britain: The AH Mk.2 is Britain's fleet of 50 AH Mk.1 Apaches rebuilt in the US to AH-64E export standard; the programme began in 2015, the first two returned in November 2020, and it entered full service on 25 March 2024, when the Mk.1 retired. Added in Update 2.51 "Spearhead", it is almost identical to the American AH-64E apart from the missing wingtip IRCM pods. Sixteen AGM-179s with 16 km range and IR or SAL guidance make stand-off attacks easy, but the outer pylons still accept only ATAS missiles, which halves its anti-tank capacity.
ah_64e_china: Taiwan ordered 30 AH-64E Apache Guardians in 2011 to supplement and later replace its AH-64Ds; deliveries ran from November 2013 to October 2014, and one was lost in fog in April 2014, the type's first hull loss, leaving 29 in service. Added in Update 2.51 "Spearhead", it matches the American AH-64E except for the missing wingtip IRCM. Its big advantage is that the outer pylons take four ATAS missiles on top of a full anti-tank load, so it carries air-to-air protection without giving up ATGMs, including up to sixteen 16 km AGM-179s with IR or SAL guidance.
ah_64e_indonesia: Indonesia chose the AH-64E in 2012 under a roughly $1.4 billion US deal for eight helicopters, weapons and support, giving its army an all-weather attack helicopter beyond its Mi-35Ps for remote areas like Papua and Kalimantan; all eight entered service in 2017 and mostly train and exercise, including Garuda Shield. Added to the Japanese tree in Update 2.51 "Spearhead", it flies and fights exactly like the US AH-64E but carries the older AN/APG-78 radar with 8 km range instead of 16 km. It also lacks DIRCM, so flares are the only answer to IR missiles.
ah_64e_netherlands: The Netherlands sent its 28 AH-64Ds to the US in November 2021 for conversion to AH-64E standard, receiving them back between 2023 and 2025. Added to the French tree in Update 2.51 "Spearhead", the Dutch AH-64E is an export model that matches the American one apart from the wingtip IRCM. Sixteen AGM-179s with 16 km range and IR or SAL guidance let it strike from well outside most threats, but the outer pylons only take ATAS missiles, so carrying air-to-air protection halves its anti-tank load.
ah_6m: The Little Bird family began with the Hughes Model 369, first flown in February 1963 for the Army's Light Observation Helicopter contest; its teardrop fuselage gave excellent visibility and its four-blade rotor great agility, and the black-painted AH-6 gunship, nicknamed the "Killer Egg", became a special-operations mainstay. Added in Update "Sky Guardians", the side-by-side two-seat AH-6M is tiny and extraordinarily agile, able to dodge in ways few helicopters can. A thermal imager and ballistic computer make it a good scout and rocket platform, and APKWS guided Hydras deal with light armour cheaply, saving Hellfires for heavier targets.
ah_mk1: AgustaWestland assembled the AH Mk.1 from Boeing kits as a British AH-64D with stronger Rolls-Royce Turbomeca engines and, on some airframes, folding blades for shipboard use; it replaced the Lynx from 2005 and fought in Afghanistan and Libya. Added in Update 1.97 "Viking Fury", it tops the British helicopter tree, outgunning and outlasting the Lynx while matching its agility, and its engines make it the fastest Apache in the game. Its Starstreak missiles are manually guided with no proximity fuse and little explosive, but countermeasures cannot fool them, so they are deadly to helicopters and even useful against light armour.
ahs: In 1995 the Swedish Army held its AttackHelikopterSystem competition between the AH-64A, Super Cobra, Mangusta, Tiger, Rooivalk, Mi-28A and Ka-50; the Apache was judged too complex and no winner was chosen. Added in Update 2.15 "Wind of Change", the Swedish AHS is the American Apache without APKWS II rockets. Twin powerful engines give it high speed and agility, it carries Hellfires, Stingers and a 30 mm cannon, and a helmet display lets the pilot aim and launch missiles with a glance. The slow Hellfires and an inaccurate cannon are its weak points.
aichi_e13a: Known as the Type 0 reconnaissance seaplane, the E13A1 was the IJN's most numerous floatplane, entering service in 1941 and serving at Pearl Harbor and Midway as well as on patrols, rescues, liaison and even kamikaze missions. Added in Update "Winged Lions", it is a catapult-launched scout for naval battles rather than a normal aircraft, with no ammunition choice or cockpit view. It can spot, cap zones, lay smoke up to three times, and drop four 60 kg bombs, more than most scout planes carry and enough to damage or sink boats and even destroyers; a single 7.7 mm gun is its only defence.
alpha_jet_a: Dornier and Dassault-Breguet developed the Alpha Jet as a Franco-German trainer and light attacker; Germany's pointed-nose Alpha Jet A, the "A" standing for appui tactique, entered service in 1979 to replace the G.91R/3, with 175 bought by 1983, before retirement in 1992 and transfer of some to Portugal. Added in Update 2.35 "Alpha Strike", it is small and agile with many external stores, best in mixed battles but dangerous in dogfights too. It has no guided weapons but a ballistic computer for rockets and bombs, a hard-hitting 27 mm Mauser BK27 in an awkward belly mount, and countermeasures; it lacks an RWR and accelerates poorly above 700 km/h.
alpha_jet_a_jabog41: JaboG 41, a West German fighter-bomber wing that traced its roots to JaboG 35 at Husum in 1959 and flew F-84Fs and G.91R/3s, converted to the Alpha Jet A in 1980, received 51 of them and disbanded in 1993 after post-reunification cuts. Added in Update 2.55 "Ninth Wave", this is a standard Alpha Jet A in JaboG 41 markings. It shares the same agility, countermeasures and wide weapon choice for mixed battles, and its small size, handling and strong cannon make it a threat in dogfights; the lack of an RWR and weak acceleration past 700 km/h remain its limits.
alpha_jet_a_thailand: Thailand agreed in the late 1990s to buy 55 ex-German Alpha Jets, but US pressure cut the deal to 25, overhauled in Germany rather than locally; they joined the 231st Squadron at Udon Thani in September 2000, around 20 kept flying, and in 2004–07 the survivors gained chaff and flare dispensers and revised pylons. Added in Update "Storm Warning", it is the familiar small, agile Alpha Jet A: excellent in mixed battles and capable in air modes thanks to its handling and cannon. A ballistic computer makes its unguided bombs and rockets accurate, and countermeasures help against IR missiles, but there is no RWR and acceleration fades above 700 km/h.
alpha_jet_e: France's version of the Dornier/Dassault-Breguet Alpha Jet, recognisable by its rounded nose, was a trainer: the French Air Force took 176 of the 303 built between 1978 and 1990 to replace T-33s, Magisters and Mystère IVs, and 75 upgraded examples still train pilots. Added in Update 2.35 "Alpha Strike", it is compact and nimble with many external stores, best in mixed battles but useful in air modes. A ballistic computer aids its unguided bombs and rockets, and the belly-mounted 30 mm DEFA 553 hits aircraft hard, with two extra gun pods available unlike the German version. It has no RWR or countermeasures and accelerates poorly above 700 km/h.
alpha_jet_th_phase_1: The Alpha Jet TH is a Royal Thai Air Force modernisation begun in 2020 with local industry, adding a digital cockpit with MFDs and HUD, new avionics and radios, the Link-T datalink, with precision weapons partly integrated, with more planned for Phase 2. Added in Update "Storm Warning", the Phase 1 version keeps the base Alpha Jet's strike role, rockets, unguided bombs and ballistic computer. It gains all-aspect AIM-9P4 missiles for self-defence but gives up its internal cannon.
am_1_mauler: Martin's AM Mauler was a wartime-ordered carrier attack aircraft built to lift as much as possible, up to 4.5 tons, but it reached service only in 1948 and lasted five years: heavy torque, difficult deck landings and leaking hydraulics turned its nickname "Able Mable" into "Awful Monster", and the Skyraider replaced it. Added in Update 1.89 "Imperial Navy", it is heavy and clumsy but carries a hard-hitting choice of HVARs, Tiny Tims and bombs of every size for ground targets. Avoid fighters, which outclass it in the air, though a well-timed turn to meet an attacker head-on can sometimes save it.
amx: The AMX, called A-11 Ghibli in Italy, was a joint Alenia, Aermacchi and Embraer design to replace Italy's G.91Ys and Brazil's MB-326s; the later ACOL upgrade gave 55 aircraft new navigation, communications and HUD plus smart weapons like JDAM, used in Afghanistan. Added in Update "Air Superiority" as the A-11A, it flies like other subsonic strike jets such as the A-6E TRAM and A-10. Six Paveway II laser-guided bombs, or eight unguided ones, make it a strong close-support aircraft, and two AIM-9Ls and internal countermeasures allow some air combat, best attempted with clean pylons.
amx_a_1a_brazil: Brazil joined Italy's AMX programme in 1981 to replace its AT-26 Xavantes, with Embraer's share covering the wings, undercarriage and drop tanks; Brazilian aircraft took two 30 mm DEFA cannons instead of the Italian gun, entered service in 1989 and were upgraded to A-1M standard in 2013. Added in Update "Seek & Destroy", the A-1A represents the pre-upgrade aircraft. Next to the Italian A-11A it brings those hard-hitting 30 mm cannons, MAA-1 Piranha air-to-air missiles and its own selection of rockets and bombs, and its guided bombs make it an excellent close-support aircraft in ground RB.
ar_2: Alexander Arkhangelsky's Ar-2, or SB-RK, reworked the SB high-speed bomber into a dive bomber in 1940 with a refined nose, smaller wings and automatic dive recovery; around 200 were built by the end of 1941 and struck German troops early in the war before the Pe-2 took over. In the game since the open beta, it is built for accurate strikes on vehicles and bases, with a wide range of bomb sizes. Rapid-fire ShKAS turrets give respectable defence and a good top speed helps it survive or escape, but it handles poorly, especially once damaged.
arado-196a-3: Arado's Ar 196 beat rival designs in 1936 to replace the Kriegsmarine's biplane shipborne floatplanes and entered production in 1938; the A-3 coastal patrol version followed in late 1940, and examples served with several Axis-aligned or occupied countries and, as captured machines, with Soviet border units into the 1950s. First a reward in the 2020 Operation S.U.M.M.E.R. event during Update "Starfighters", it now serves as a ship-launched scout in naval battles. Two 20 mm MG FF cannons, an MG 17, two 50 kg bombs and a rear 7.92 mm gun make it well armed for a low-rank floatplane, and like other seaplanes it can capture points.
arado-196a-5: The Ar 196 A-5 of 1943 brought MG FF/M cannons, twin MG 81Z defensive guns with more ammunition, extra crew armour and new instruments; Finland bought 15 for reconnaissance and light bombing, while Sweden's single example, captured in 1943, was operated by British intelligence through a private firm and crashed in 1947. Added to the Swedish tree in Update 2.19 "Drone Age", this Finnish aircraft improves on the German A-3's rear defence. It hits hard, defends itself well and can land on water, but it runs short of cannon shells quickly and any biplane fighter out-turns it.
arado-234: The first jet bomber anywhere and the Luftwaffe's second jet type in service, Arado's Ar 234 came too late and in too few numbers to matter; it was fast and flew high, yet a poor rearward view and sluggish low-speed handling let slower Allied fighters catch some. The B-2 carried up to 1,500 kg of bombs, usually three 500 kg SC500s, or a single 1,000 kg bomb instead, and was fitted with a Patin autopilot and a complex tachymetric bombsight that could work together. It has been in the game since the open beta.
arado-234c-3: Troubles with the Jumo 004 led Arado to try the lighter BMW 003, and the Ar 234 C used four of them, along with airframe and visibility improvements, to reach an impressive 857 km/h; only a handful were built amid Germany's final collapse. Added in Update 1.49 "Weapons of Victory", the C-3 gets a bomber air spawn, two nose-mounted MG 151 cannons with plenty of ammunition, and speed that makes it both a quick bomber and a useful heavy fighter. Its three bombs hang outside and cause a lot of drag, there is no airbrake for diving on bases, and the controls stiffen badly at high speed.
arado_234b_2_mt: The B-2 was the dedicated bomber model of Arado's pioneering jet; it first flew in March 1944 with its bombs carried externally because fuel filled the fuselage; around 210 Ar 234s were built, and the WB 151 Magirusbombe gun pod, designed for night-fighter variants that never entered production, was sometimes fitted to day bombers. Added in Update 2.59 "Sky Odyssey", this version survives damage well and carries a decent bomb load. The extra cannons, together with good handling, let it fight enemy fighters effectively, but its engines are relatively weak and the pilot is poorly protected.
ariete: Aerfer developed the Ariete as an export follow-up to the Sagittario 2, which had lost to the G.91 in NATO's contest; a new engine made it one of the most agile jets of its day, but it found no buyers and the company moved on to the Leone. Added in Update "Danger Zone", it is among the best dogfighters in the Italian tree, with excellent handling and a pair of rapid-firing cannons that destroy anything they hit. Its supplementary engine is weak on its own but noticeably improves performance, while a small fuel load limits time aloft, so avoid overextending.
attaker_fb1: Supermarine's Attacker began as a jet conversion of the Spiteful, the planned Spitfire successor, adapted for the Royal Navy; it became the Navy's first operational carrier jet, and the last 11 F.1s were converted into FB.1 fighter-bombers. Added in Update 1.49 "Weapons of Victory", it comes after the Sea Fury among Fleet Air Arm aircraft and can fight in the air or attack ground targets. Its four 20 mm Hispano Mk V cannons sit in the wings, unusual among British jets of its time, so convergence needs setting as on the Sea Fury, and two bombs or 12 rockets make it a quick fighter-bomber.
attaker_fb2: The Attacker FB.2 followed the FB.1 with a new Rolls-Royce Nene engine and other changes; 84 were built, but as Britain's first naval jet the Attacker was soon outclassed by more powerful designs and gone from service by 1954. A premium since Update "Ixwa Strike", it barely differs from the tech-tree FB 1, offering the same early-jet strengths: a solid engine that lets it position for attacks on aircraft or for dropping ordnance on ground targets. It is a sensible way to learn the jump from piston to jet flying.
av_8a: Seeking an A-4 replacement for amphibious close support, the US Marines adopted the Harrier, licence-built by McDonnell Douglas as the AV-8A (Harrier Mk 50 to Hawker Siddeley); the first arrived in March 1971 and the type served until 1987. Added in Update "New Power" as among the US tree's earliest VTOL jets, it uses its vectoring nozzles for vertical take-off and landing and for extra agility. It shares the GR.3 and AV-8C's engine, stronger than the GR.1's, and can carry Sidewinders, bombs, rockets or a mix of them, making it very flexible.
av_8b_na: The AV-8B Night Attack variant, first planned as the AV-8D, added a Hughes AN/ASB-19 FLIR in the nose, colour moving maps and other systems for accurate strikes by night and in poor weather; all early AV-8Bs were later upgraded to either this or the radar-equipped AV-8B+. Added in Update "Dance of Dragons", it outclasses the Sea Harrier FRS.1 almost everywhere despite lacking radar or BVR missiles, thanks to strong flight performance, good IR missiles and VIFF tricks that win slow dogfights. Ground attack is its real forte: Paveways, AGM-65E2 and G Mavericks, JDAMs, a targeting pod, a fast-firing 25 mm GAU-12 and plentiful countermeasures.
av_8b_plus: The AV-8B Plus was developed alongside the Night Attack Harrier for air-to-air work, replacing the nose FLIR with an AN/APG-65 radar taken from F/A-18s being upgraded to the APG-73, which brought AIM-120 AMRAAM capability and newer Sidewinders so it could escort other Harriers. Added in Update "Seek & Destroy", it is a genuine all-rounder whose only real handicap is being subsonic among supersonic opponents. AMRAAMs, smokeless IRCCM AIM-9Ms, a multi-mode radar and the GAU-12 cannon make it lethal in the air, and with a LITENING II pod it can drop up to ten laser- or GPS-guided bombs or fire Mavericks. Easy to learn, it rewards practice.
av_8b_plus_italy: Once a 1989 ban on fixed-wing naval aviation was lifted, Italy ordered 14 AV-8B+ and two TAV-8B trainers in 1990 for the carrier Giuseppe Garibaldi; most were assembled locally by Alenia, they first deployed to Somalia in 1995, and they now fly from the Cavour pending F-35Bs. Added in Update "Sons of Attila", it is a strong all-rounder: useful as a support fighter in air battles and devastating in mixed ones with up to ten GBU-12s and a LITENING II pod, Mavericks or GBU-16s, a GAU-12 cannon and a pair of AIM-9Ms. VIFFing forces overshoots in dogfights, and it can even hover behind cover to launch Mavericks like a helicopter.
av_8c: To bridge the gap until enough Harrier IIs arrived, the US Marines upgraded 47 AV-8As to AV-8C standard from 1979, adding a radar warning receiver, built-in countermeasures, new avionics and a longer service life; both versions retired in 1987. Added alongside the AV-8A in Update "New Power", it flies and fights almost exactly like its predecessor, with the same vertical take-off and landing ability. The internal dispenser holds fewer countermeasures than the AV-8A's pod but frees a hardpoint for weapons, and the RWR warns when radar is tracking it, making it a more capable strike fighter overall.
av_8s_late_thailand: Thailand bought the carrier Chakri Nareubet from Spain in 1992 along with ten AV-8S Matadors, export first-generation Harriers, creating Southeast Asia's only carrier air wing; they arrived in 1998 just as the Asian financial crisis hit, spare parts dried up and the jets were retired after eight years. Added to Japan's Thai sub-tree in Update "Storm Warning", the AV-8S Late shows them near the end of service. It performs much like the Sea Harrier FRS.1 squadron vehicle, with up to four AIM-9Ls, but swaps the radar for a broader payload including napalm and a large countermeasure pod.
av_8s_thailand: Spain ordered the AV-8S Matador in 1972 for the carrier Dédalo, with deliveries routed via the US to get round a British embargo, and flew them until 1989; Thailand then took ten for its new carrier Chakri Narubet for anti-piracy patrols in the Gulf of Thailand, but without spares only one could fly by 1999 and they were retired in 2006. Added to Japan's Thai sub-tree in Update "Firebirds", this early-service AV-8S resembles the British Harrier GR.1 with improvements: a pair of AIM-9Ps, a large countermeasure pod and an RWR. Like the later version, it shines at low level, using VTOL tricks to surprise enemies.
avenger_mk1: The Avenger Mk II was the Royal Navy's name for the TBF-1C, supplied under Lend-Lease from 1942 to replace obsolete Swordfish and Albacore biplanes; 958 Avengers of all marks went to Britain, 334 of them C models. Added in Update 1.39, it is well protected and shrugs off long bursts from rifle-calibre guns, and a dorsal .50 cal turret bites back. Two forward .50 cals, bombs up to 2,000 lb, torpedoes and a pair of Uncle Tom rockets give it plenty of options against tanks, bases and ships. Its ventral 7.62 mm gun covers little, and it flies poorly next to enemy fighters.
aw_159: AgustaWestland's AW159 Wildcat grew from the "Future Lynx" programme to replace British Lynx and Gazelle helicopters, becoming a new design in the mid-2000s with a glass cockpit, new radar, RWR, countermeasures and CTS800 engines; the Royal Navy flies the HMA2, and Algeria, the Philippines and South Korea have also bought it. Added in Update 2.59 "Sky Odyssey", it carries as many as 20 Martlet missiles, small-warhead but fast with about 6 km of range and usable against light vehicles and aircraft, plus Spike NLOS for heavy armour. Powerful engines make it agile enough to dodge missiles, but it has little armour, so watch for return fire.
b-17e: The first Flying Fortress built in quantity, the B-17E (512 delivered) gained a 3 m longer fuselage, a larger tail, a new tail gun position and Sperry turrets, plus uprated Cyclone engines to cope with about 20% more weight. In the game since the open beta, it is the first heavy bomber of the US tree. More than ten 12.7 mm guns spread across several turrets give strong defence, and as much as 8,000 lb of bombs can destroy two bombing points. The wings are fragile, so avoid hard turns that could overload them.
b-17e_japan: This is most likely B-17E 41-2471, abandoned by the 7th Bomb Group after it crash-landed on Java in February 1942, then repaired by the Japanese with parts from other wrecks and flown to Tachikawa for study and training; its final fate is unknown. Added in Update 1.43, it works as a level bomber from height against airfields, bases and other strategic targets, not moving tanks, which scatter and are hard to hit from height. Climb to 4,000 m or more, fly in formation with other bombers for mutual protection, and ideally have fighters sweeping ahead to deal with interceptors.
b-17e_late: The B-17E/L, in the game since the open beta, is a high-altitude bomber meant for fortifications, airfields and bases rather than moving vehicles, which dodge falling bombs and are hard to hit from height. Unlike the earlier B-17E it has a Sperry ball turret under the belly, closing the gap below, and it is better armoured than earlier B-17s. The nose is still its weak spot, defended only by .30 cal guns that struggle in an uptier, so link up with other bombers after spawning.
b-17g: The B-17G of 1943 was the main production Flying Fortress, with around 8,680 built, adding a remote chin turret, better cheek guns, staggered waist positions, improved superchargers and the roomier "Cheyenne" tail turret. In the game since the open beta, it is quicker and climbs better at altitude than the B-17E, and its extra guns leave almost no blind spots. Wing racks add a pair of 1,000 or 2,000 lb bombs, so it hits bases harder. The family's weaknesses remain: a fragile tail, high wing loading that limits manoeuvring, and a tendency to burn.
b-17g_iaf: In 1948 the IAF obtained three unarmed civilian B-17s, flew them to Czechoslovakia to fit 7.62 mm guns, improvised bombsights and German bomb racks, and had them bomb targets on the way to Israel; they flew 200 sorties in the 1948 war, served as radio relay aircraft in 1956 and retired in 1958. Added with the first Israeli aircraft in Update "Winged Lions", it is vulnerable to almost anything, especially air-spawning or fast-climbing fighters such as Bf 109s, Ta 152Hs and F8F-1Bs. Climb above 6,000 m before the base run, and point the tail at threats, since the nose is its weakest side.
b-29: Boeing's B-29 answered the need for a bomber with the range and payload for the Pacific, adding a pressurised cabin for high-altitude flight, a ceiling near 9,750 m, about 600 km/h and up to 9,000 kg of bombs; its General Electric central fire control let gunners aim remote turrets with computed lead, sometimes several at once. Added in Update 1.47 "Big Guns", it is purely a bomber, carrying up to forty 500 lb, eighteen 1,000 lb, eight 2,000 lb or four 4,000 lb bombs for base raids or carpet bombing. Altitude keeps it safe, and twelve .50 cals with excellent coverage punish persistent interceptors.
b-57: Carrying no guns at all, the B-57A jet bomber, added in Update 1.43, relies on speed to survive: its two J65 turbojets push it to 902 km/h stock and 950 km/h fully upgraded, faster than many fighters. The airframe tolerates +12 g, more than most opponents can pull, allowing very tight high-g turns, but only −6 g, so avoid pushing the nose down hard. Nine 500 lb or six 1,000 lb bombs make a reasonable payload, though nothing like a B-29's.
b-57b: Martin's B-57B was the second licence-built Canberra, adding eight .50 cal guns (later four 20 mm M39 cannons), a fighter-style cockpit with better visibility, a rotary bomb bay, improved airbrakes, four extra wing pylons and an RWR; 202 were built and served through Vietnam until 1983. Added in Update 1.47 "Big Guns", it beats the B-57A almost everywhere, with real guns, better turning and bigger loads including rockets and napalm. The stock wing-mounted .50s are poor against aircraft, but the M39 upgrade hits harder than the Canberra B (I) Mk 6's guns. Alone it is easy prey for MiG-15s and Sabres, so coordinate with teammates.
b5n2: Known as the Type 97 carrier attack bomber, the B5N2 served as the IJN's standard torpedo and level bomber, first flown in 1937 and faster than its Allied counterparts; it fought at Pearl Harbor, Midway, the Coral Sea and Santa Cruz and, as its B6N replacement was delayed, served in secondary roles until 1945. In the game since the open beta, the B5N2 is a large target thanks to its wide wings, yet it is agile and quick enough to outfly many interceptors. It carries a useful range of ordnance for level bombing at height or low down, and for attacking ships.
b6n1: The Tenzan 11 was meant to replace the B5N, but engine and stability problems delayed it from a first flight in March 1941 to service in August 1943, and inexperienced crews and US air superiority blunted it in combat. Added in Update "Starfighters", it is faster and longer-ranged than the B5N2 but lifts the same weight: one 800 kg torpedo or bomb, a pair of 250 kg bombs or six 60 kg bombs. Its rear 7.7 mm guns, including a ventral one, mostly just deter, while an odd forward 7.7 mm in the left wing, meant for suppressing ship AA, can down aircraft thanks to its agility.
b6n2: The Tenzan 12 resulted from an order to standardise naval engines, so Nakajima replaced the Mamoru with the 1,850 hp Mitsubishi Kasei 25, lengthening the nose and fitting a smaller four-blade propeller, a fixed tailwheel and multiple exhaust stacks; engine availability made it the most numerous Tenzan. Added in Update "Starfighters", it is only marginally faster than the B6N1 and otherwise identical, with the same agility, ordnance and weak rear guns. It loses the B6N1's odd forward-firing 7.7 mm, so unlike that model or the up-gunned B6N2a it is a poor choice for engaging aircraft.
b6n2a: The Tenzan 12 Kō replaced the standard model's two 7.7 mm guns with a 13 mm Type 2 and a 7.92 mm Type 1, Japanese derivatives of the German MG 131 and MG 15, and carried an H-6 anti-ship radar with Yagi antennas on the wings and rear fuselage. Added in Update "Starfighters", it keeps the Tenzan's agility, so fighters that underestimate a bomber with no forward guns can be out-turned and punished from the rear. Its main job is still torpedo and level bombing with one large bomb or torpedo, two 250 kg bombs or six 60 kg bombs.
b7a2: Aichi designed the B7A2 Ryusei to replace both the Tenzan and the Suisei as a carrier torpedo and dive bomber, featuring inverted gull wings and a Homare 12 engine; first flying in May 1942, it suffered engine and airframe troubles, so only 114 were built, and they saw little action, mostly from land bases. Added in Update 1.37, it is surprisingly fast and agile for its size but unarmoured. Two wing cannons and a rear 13 mm gun let it fight back, and four extra 60 kg wing bombs supplement its bay, so it plays like a versatile attacker with an accurate gyro-stabilised dive sight.
b7a2_homare_23: This Ryusei was a prototype fitted with the Homare 23 engine, 200 hp stronger than the production Homare 12, but otherwise unchanged; it never entered mass production. A Battle Pass Season XII reward ("Armour Breaking Ambusher") from Update "La Royale", it handles like the B7A2 with extra power, still without real armour. Twin Type 99 Model 2 wing cannons and a rear 13 mm gun suit both head-on attacks and defence, and it can dive-, level- or torpedo-bomb, adding four 60 kg wing bombs to a bay that holds either a pair of 250 kg or half a dozen 60 kg bombs.
b_10b: The Martin B-10 changed bomber design: first flown in February 1932, it combined an all-metal monoplane structure, enclosed cockpits, a gun turret, retractable undercarriage and an internal bay, and was the first bomber built in quantity that could outrun contemporary fighters. 348 were built, with exports to Argentina, China, Thailand, Turkey and the Netherlands. A premium since Update 1.67 "Assault", it carries a large bomb load for its rank, but the aircraft it faces are more modern and faster. Its good agility in the horizontal plane helps it evade attackers.
b_18a: Douglas based the B-18 on the DC-2 airliner as the Martin B-10's successor, and it briefly became the backbone of USAAC bomber units, but by 1940 it was seen as slow, underpowered, poorly armed and lightly protected; many were wrecked on the ground at Pearl Harbor. Added in Update 1.59 "Flaming Arrows", it is the US tree's first land-based bomber with more than one engine, carrying 2,000 lb of bombs. Only the dorsal gunner has a useful arc of fire, and the tail blocks the area directly behind. Its poor handling makes high-altitude level bombing the best approach.
b_239_finland: In 1939 Finland ordered the B-239, a land-based export F2A-1 Buffalo that was lighter without its carrier gear, with a slightly stronger engine and four machine guns; it arrived too late for the Winter War but served through the Continuation War, where LeLv 24 claimed 477 Soviet aircraft for the loss of 19. Added to the Swedish tree in Update "Fire and Ice", it is dangerous even for less experienced pilots thanks to its handling and firepower. Flown like a Bf 109 with boom-and-zoom attacks, it can also turn-fight better than the Messerschmitt, and not just when fast.
b_24d: Consolidated was asked to licence-build the B-17 but proposed its own bomber instead: the B-24 Liberator, whose thick, efficient Davis wing gave it speed, range and payload, with deliveries from 1941. 18,188 were built, the most of any bomber, though crews found it hard to fly and fragile, its wing prone to snapping off when hit. In the game since the open beta, the B-24D is faster and climbs better than the B-17 and carries a similar load internally, but turns like a brick and is far more vulnerable, so keep a constant watch for fighters.
b_25j_1: North American's B-25 grew from the NA-40 and a 1939 Army call for a fast medium bomber, becoming the archetype of the type: over 10,000 were built, served in every theatre and under Lend-Lease with China and the USSR, and famously launched from a carrier for the Doolittle Raid on Japan. The B-25J-1, added in Update 1.29, is a flexible bomber or attacker suited to many styles. Its twin-.50 tail turret is well known for setting pursuing fighters on fire, buying time to reach the target.
b_25j_20: Later B-25s shifted from pure bombing towards low-level attack, trading glazed noses for extra guns, in some cases a 75 mm cannon, skimming treetops and ship masts, and taking more cockpit armour at the expense of bomb load. Fast for its size, carrying over 3,000 lb and defended from nearly every angle, the Mitchell became the model medium bomber. In the game since Update 1.29, the B-25J-20 works as a bomber, a strafer or both, and its twin .50 cal tail guns have a reputation for punishing fighters that settle behind it.
b_25j_30_china: China was among the Lend-Lease recipients of the B-25 Mitchell, a twin-engine bomber designed to a 1939 US Army requirement for 2,400 lb carried 1,200 miles at around 300 mph; it beat those figures and became the classic medium bomber, with more than 10,000 built. Added in Update 1.91 "Night Vision", the Chinese B-25J-30 can serve as a level bomber, a low-level strafer or both, adapting to different playstyles. Gunners cover most angles, and the twin .50 cal tail position is especially good at discouraging fighters on its tail.
b_25j_30_vvs_ussr: The USSR received about 800 B-25s under Lend-Lease from 1942, flying them by day, night and in bad weather as long-range and tactical bombers and even to supply partisans; crews valued their speed, toughness, payload, radios and bombsight, and they served until 1953, later training Tu-4 crews thanks to similar landing gear. Added in Update 1.35, the Soviet B-25J-30 carries FAB-50 to FAB-500 bombs for base bombing or ground targets. Six forward-firing 12.7 mm guns, closely grouped, are deadly for strafing and in head-on passes, and seven more defensive .50 cals punish close pursuers.
b_26b_c: Martin's B-26 Marauder, built for speed and range, entered service in 1941 with short wings and a high stall speed that caused many fatal landings and nicknames like "Widowmaker"; after a 1942 Truman Committee ultimatum, the B-26B gained longer wings and a bigger tail, and the type went on to lose proportionally fewer aircraft than any other USAAF bomber, with "Flak-Bait" surviving 207 sorties. Added in Update "Wind of Change", it bridges the B-25 and B-17E, with Mitchell-style forward guns for strafing and a size and payload nearer the Fortress. It is sluggish but carries heavy ordnance for ground or naval targets.
b_26b_indonesia_kalong: After shooting down a CIA-operated B-26B supporting rebels in 1958, Indonesia ordered six of the Douglas Invaders in 1959 and used them against the Permesta rebellion, in Operation Trikora and during the 1963–66 Konfrontasi, retiring them in December 1977 as the last B-26 operator. Added to the Japanese tree in Update 2.59 "Sky Odyssey", it is a ground attacker with hard-hitting guns, plenty of underwing weapons and a good climb rate for its class. It is large and clumsy with only one defensive gunner, and stands out for an unusual mix of weapons, Soviet bombs among them, plus new rocket types.
b_26c_france: After the 1942 Torch landings, French units swapped their LeO 451s and DB-7s for B-26C Marauders and flew them over Italy and the south of France; one later became a flying testbed for SNECMA's first Atar jets. Added in Update "Wind of Change", it is effectively the American B-26B in French colours, the C designation marking long-wing aircraft built at Omaha rather than Baltimore. It sits between the giant N.C.223.3 at one end and quick, lightly armed types such as the LeO 451 at the other: sluggish, but with near-heavy-bomber protection and payload for bases, columns or close support.
b_34: Lockheed's Ventura was a larger, more powerful Hudson successor derived from the Lodestar airliner and used mainly by the RAF; the Lend-Lease Ventura IIA became the B-34 Lexington in US service, where most were kept to training. Added in Update 1.65 "Way of the Samurai", it improves on the Hudson with up to 2,500 lb of bombs and stronger defence from twin 12.7 mm and twin 7.62 mm turrets with plenty of ammunition. Two forward 12.7 mm and two 7.62 mm guns can strafe or engage aircraft, and a structural limit above 630 km/h lets it dive quickly onto bases.
b_48_firecrest: Blackburn's Firecrest (YA.1) was a naval strike fighter developed from the troubled Firebrand; design changes, missing components and stalled engine development delayed it until 1947, by which time jets had overtaken it, and only two of three prototypes flew. Among the earliest squadron vehicles, added in Update 1.89 "Imperial Navy", it resembles a cross between the Firebrand and the Corsair, with gull wings, a strong engine and a sturdy airframe. Two wing-mounted heavy machine guns and an 18-inch Mk XV torpedo suit it to naval battles more than air combat, and airbrakes and an arrestor hook allow carrier operations.
b_52h: Boeing's B-52 Stratofortress answered a 1946 call for a long-range bomber; the final B-52H, first flown in July 1960 with fuel-efficient TF33 turbofans, an M61 cannon in place of machine guns and aerial refuelling, was built until 1962 (102 aircraft) and has flown from Vietnam to strikes on Iran in 2026, remaining in USAF service. It arrived as a reward from the 2026 "Nuclear Thunder" event. Reasonably fast and able to carry as much as 30 tons of ordnance, it defends itself only with a 20 mm cannon, an RWR and countermeasures, which is not much for such a huge target, so it relies on teammates.
b_66b: Douglas adapted the Navy's A-3 Skywarrior into the B-66 Destroyer for the US Air Force, but extensive redesign brought weaker J71 engines and new low-level bombing systems, along with the ejection seats the A-3 lacked; 294 B-66s were built, 72 as B-66B bombers, and the last retired in 1975. Added in Update 2.49 "Tusk Force", it carries plenty of bombs and has a powerful tail turret for protection.
